stories.title: Israel vows to get to 'root' of man behind plane attack
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel will get to the "root" of the co-pilot who engaged ⁠in a foiled attempt to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight and that Israel will "possibly" be participating in the probe into the incident. Mr Netanyahu said it ⁠was too early to say who was behind the foiled bid to crash the flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. "It's too early to say, the attacking pilot is .. now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I think he'll be taken ‌to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at ⁠least where he left, ‌where he flew off from, and we'll be ⁠following ‌and possibly also participating in this investigation," Mr Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News. Mr Netanyahu's comment came in response to a question about whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement in the incident. Passengers on the flydubai flight reached Israel safely after passengers and crew foiled a co-pilot's attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, in a struggle that began when he stabbed the pilot ⁠and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. Passengers and crew entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and enabled a second pair of flydubai pilots who were aboard the flight to land the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, according to Israeli officials.

stories.title: Over 100,000 public sector workers begin work-to-rule
stories.summary: More than 100,000 public sector workers in areas such as health, education and local authorities have begun industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule. Nurses, civil servants and special needs assistants are among those taking part in the action over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said the work-to-rule means that its members in the public health service will perform only duties and responsibilities necessary for safe patient care during their rostered hours. "INMO members will not work any additional unpaid hours," the union said. "They will not attend non-clinical meetings, except where attendance is strictly necessary for direct patient care," the INMO added. The action will also involve Fórsa, the country's largest public sector union, and will see special needs assistants, health workers, civil servants and local authority employees refuse to do additional work outside of their normal duties.

stories.title: Irish players 'exposed, hung out to dry' by FAI - Ennis
stories.summary: Social Democrats TD and Spokesperson on Sport Daniel Ennis has said the Ireland players "have been hung out to dry" by the FAI and the board of the association should resign. The FAI is to tell the Oireachtas Sports Committee today how the decision to proceed with the controversial fixtures against Israel was made in the best interests of Irish football. The CEO of the FAI David Courell and other senior figures at the Association will answer questions from TDs and Senators this afternoon with Ireland to play Israel again on Sunday in the UEFA Nations League after preparations for last weekend's fixture in Hungary were thrown into chaos at the eleventh hour. He said it is the biggest crisis facing Irish football, with many people telling him that they will not renew season tickets. Mr Ennis said that the FAI has put "a dark stain" on Irish football. In relation to possible sanctions that the FAI may have faced for not playing the match, Mr Ennis said that "no sanction stands up against the charred remains of babies."

stories.title: Manufacturing output hits more than four year high - PMI
stories.summary: The manufacturing sector accelerated in September as production grew at its fastest pace since March 2022 and demand remained firm in domestic and overseas markets, a business survey showed today. The latest AIB Ireland Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, rose to 55.5 in September from 55.4 in August, a survey by S&P Global showed. "Output rose rapidly in September, increasing to the highest level since March 2022, with respondents citing continued robust order books," said David McNamara, AIB's chief economist. Production growth was the sharpest since March 2022, and new orders rose for a 21st month in a row. Total new work expanded at a slightly softer rate than August's 52-month high. Export orders increased, with the seasonally adjusted New Export Orders Index reaching its highest level since June. Firms cited stronger business inflows from major developed markets. Employment growth was unchanged from August's seven-month low.

stories.title: Pilot tried to crash Tel Aviv-bound plane - Netanyahu
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the co-pilot of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv tried to crash the plane after stabbing the pilot, but passengers then held him down while other pilots landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. Describing the event as "a highly severe security incident," Mr Netanyahu said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 from the United Arab Emirates to Israel. The alleged assailant, who an Israeli official identified as an Omani national, was arrested after the plane landed, Mr Netanyahu said. "All passengers are out of harm's way," Mr Netanyahu, who described the passengers as being almost all Israeli, said in a video statement released by his office. The Israeli leader quoted a passenger as saying that passengers along with a member of the crew broke into the cockpit after the aircraft "entered a tailspin and began to dive" and found the co-pilot "trying to sabotage the plane's systems". "They saved many lives. They prevented a heavy disaster," he said.

stories.title: Preview: Ireland to face pressing questions from Austria
stories.summary: For Heimir Hallgrimsson, one short aside on Wednesday highlighted what the Republic of Ireland manager would ideally have wanted to speak about on the eve of a match. "We are in a pre-match press conference before a game against Austria and we have hardly ever spoken about football here," he said. But this has been a window like no other. As expected, the tenor of the pre-match press conference questions was going to focus on the controversial UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel and the fallout from Saturday's acrimonious build-up to the first of those matches in Debrecen. The Israel issue will still be front and centre again tonight at Aviva Stadium. The Stop The Game campaign have promised that protests will take place around the game with the visiting Austrians. Four months ago, the same campaign staged a tennis ball protest in the same venue during a friendly against Qatar. It's unclear what shape tonight's protests will take, nor what the overall attendance figures will be. And that's not even to countenance how players will be received individually and collectively from those in the stands.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice leading candidate to succeed Joyce in Galway
stories.summary: Éamonn Fitzmaurice is in advanced talks with the Galway County Board to take over the manager's position vacated by Pádraic Joyce in early September. It is understood the Finuge clubman has engaged positively with Galway chairman Paul Bellew in recent weeks and is the leading candidate to take charge of the Tribesmen's senior footballers. A three-time All-Ireland winner as a player, Fitzmaurice managed Kerry for six years between 2013 and 2018, leading the Kingdom to Sam Maguire glory in 2014. He also claimed six straight Munster SFC titles and an Allianz League title during his time in charge. He remained involved with the club scene in his native Kerry, coaching the Clifford brothers' club Fossa in 2022 as they claimed a junior All-Ireland title. He was one of the most prominent members of the Football Review Committee, which introduced, trialled and refined the new playing rules that many see as having a revitalising effect on the game since their introduction in 2015.

stories.title: Stop The Game issue open letter to Ireland squad
stories.summary: The Stop The Game campaign have issued an open letter to Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson and his squad, asking them to not to participate in Sunday's Nations League fixture against Israel. Sunday's game is technically the home fixture against Israel, but will be played in Serbia amid continue unrest among supporters that the game is being played. Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu opted out of the squad for last weekend's 3-0 victory against Israel, stressing his belief that he felt it was wrong to play due to the atrocities in the region. Bazunu is back for Thursday's home game against Austria, but with Ireland again due to face Israel this weekend, Stop The Game have renewed their calls for the players and management to boycott the game. The letter read: "We are writing to appeal to each of you, individually and collectively, not to take part in Sunday's fixture against Israel in Serbia. "We want to begin by acknowledging Gavin Bazunu. His decision not to be available for these fixtures was an act of immense personal courage. It was a humanitarian stance, taken at professional risk, and it has received admiration around the world. He has honoured Irish football and he has honoured Ireland.

stories.title: Payne embedding a 'strike to score' mentality at Munster
stories.summary: Like every coach, Jared Payne has his own philosophy in how he sees the game. "Play fast. Strike to score quickly. Play smart." It all sounds pretty simple, but having a philosophy and implementing one at the top level is a whole other ball game. Payne made the move back to Ireland over the summer, having spent time with Clermont and the Scarlets following his departure from Ulster back in 2022. His new role sees him in tandem with fellow attack coach Mossy Lawler, as they work together to try and break down opposing defences. The task at hand was bound to be steep, succeeding Mike Prendergast who helped Munster to URC glory in 2023, and who had been widely viewed as a potential future head coach at the province. On the field, the Kiwi works on phases one to three, or your traditional striking phases; with Lawler taking the general phase play which follows. It is a setup which mirrors what Ireland have with Andy Farrell and Andrew Goodman, as the dual-coach role becomes more normal in the modern game. When asked for what he wants from his side, he laid all of his cards on the table speaking to the media on Tuesday. "Play fast. Strike to score quickly. Play smart," he outlined as his core principles.

stories.title: Druid explores O'Neill's A Moon for the Misbegotten
stories.summary: Patrick Lonergan explores the history of Eugene O'Neill's theatrical masterpiece A Moon for the Misbegotten, revived by Druid Theatre Company and coming to Gaiety Theatre this October for the Dublin Theatre Festival. A Moon for the Misbegotten was the last play that Eugene O'Neill ever completed, and its elegiac tone makes it feel like it might have been his own unconscious farewell to playwriting. He described his play as a "fine, unusual, tragic comedy" – and its blend of humour and sadness is indeed both fine and unusual. The play is deeply autobiographical, drawing on the figure of O’Neill’s brother Jamie, an actor who had drunk himself to death when he was only 45. Reimagining his brother as James Tyrone, O’Neill confines that character to a single place and a single 24-hour-period, so that he can grapple with the possibility of finding love with Josie, a young Irish-American woman. What follows is a battle between both characters’ competing desires: for love, reputation, ownership of land – and for just one more drink. Irishness is central to those conflicts. The play’s stage directions say of Josie that the "map of Ireland is stamped on her face" – an old Irish-American saying that was intended to suggest distinctively Irish features. But in one of many connections between the two characters, the same phrasing is used to describe Tyrone too – not in Moon but in A Long Day’s Journey Into Night, a companion play that O’Neill wrote between 1939 and 1941, but which was not staged until after his death. That link reveals O’Neill’s desire to present Tyrone and Josie both as psychologically complex individuals and as emblematically Irish. Writing about them thus became a way for him to map Ireland, and to think about its multifaceted influence on American life. That theme is apparent from the first act, when Josie and her father – a tenant farmer called Phil Hogan – are trying to frighten off a neighbouring landowner. They do so by playing on the stereotypes associated with their nationality: they are buoyant and comical – but also menacing, as if their buffoonery could tip into violence at any moment. They are, in other words, like characters in a stage Irish play.

A Moon for the Misbegotten was the last play that Eugene O'Neill ever completed, and its elegiac tone makes it feel like it might have been his own unconscious farewell to playwriting. He described his play as a "fine, unusual, tragic comedy" – and its blend of humour and sadness is indeed both fine and unusual. The play is deeply autobiographical, drawing on the [[duine mór|figure]] of O’Neill’s [[deartháir|brother]] Jamie, an actor who had drunk himself to death when he was only 45. Reimagining his [[deartháir|brother]] as James Tyrone, O’Neill confines that character to a single place and a single 24-hour-period, so that he can grapple with the [[féidearthacht|possibility]] of finding love with Josie, a [[óg|young]] Irish-American woman. What follows is a battle between both characters’ competing desires: for love, reputation, ownership of land – and for just one more drink. Irishness is central to those [[coinbhleachtaí|conflicts]]. The play’s stage directions say of Josie that the "map of Ireland is stamped on her face" – an old Irish-American saying that was intended to suggest distinctively Irish features. But in one of many connections between the two characters, the same phrasing is used to describe Tyrone too – not in Moon but in A Long Day’s Journey Into Night, a companion play that O’Neill wrote between 1939 and 1941, but which was not staged until after his [[bás|death]]. That link reveals O’Neill’s desire to present Tyrone and Josie both as psychologically complex individuals and as emblematically Irish. Writing about them thus became a way for him to map Ireland, and to think about its multifaceted influence on American life. That theme is apparent from the first act, when Josie and her [[athair|father]] – a tenant [[feirmeoir|farmer]] called Phil Hogan – are trying to frighten off a neighbouring landowner. They do so by playing on the stereotypes associated with their [[náisiúntacht|nationality]]: they are buoyant and comical – but also menacing, as if their buffoonery could tip into [[foréigean|violence]] at any [[nóiméad|moment]]. They are, in other words, like characters in a [[ardán|stage]] Irish play.

stories.title: Guests revealed for 2 Johnnies Late Night Lock In
stories.summary: Returning for its fourth series, the new run will also see the return of The Parish Quiz, which this week features Jack English from Adare, Co. Limerick playing against Laura Collins of Scartaglen, Co. Kerry. Zamparelli will talk about her television career, revisit her hidden-camera antics on The Fear, and share stories about married life with her husband, Lau. Regan will explain the difference between "a gob****e and an eejit", share his experiences of being an Irishman abroad, and reveal why the Irish accent is a superpower overseas. Paddy McDonnell joins the show from Belfast to perform a stand-up set, and Galway trad act Clada will play Step It Out Mary. Speaking about the new season, Johnny Smacks says, "We're absolutely delighted to be back for Season 4 of The Late Night Lock In. When we started the show, the idea was basically to bring the craic of a great Irish night out onto the telly - a bit of music, brilliant guests, plenty of messing and absolutely no guarantee that Johnny B will stick to the running order. Johnny B adds, "The best thing about The Late Night Lock In is that it doesn’t feel like a normal TV show. It feels like you’ve landed into a pub on a Thursday night, found yourself sitting beside someone you never expected to meet, the band starts playing and suddenly you’re staying for one more.

stories.title: This is why spider season has started early this year
stories.summary: Cosy season is well and truly here, with the chillier weather and blustery showers encouraging us to swap the t-shirts and shorts of summer for the comfort of our sofas. And we're not the only ones taking shelter from the elements indoors: the spiders are at it, too. Our eight-legged friends have reached their mating season, which leads them to move indoors, taking up residence in nooks, crannies, presses and more around the home. "Spider season is fantastic", claims Collie Ennis, a possibly deeply unpopular opinion but one entirely fitting the Biodiversity Officer and Zoology research associate at Trinity College Dublin. "They're all big and bold and they’re out and about, and it’s quite exciting if you’re a bit of a spider nerd", he added, speaking like a spider nerd. By way of explaining this influx of arachnids, Ennis says that this season comes after they’re spent the summer maturing and waiting to breed. "It’s been a good summer for bugs, with the heat and the humidity", he adds. "So they’ve kind of gotten big and bold very fast."

stories.title: US woman on death row survives two lethal injections
stories.summary: Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Pike to death yesterday for a 1995 murder despite administering two doses of a lethal drug. Pike was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her lawyers said. "We have not been informed as to her condition," Pike's lawyers said in a statement. Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am local time yesterday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later, the US Supreme Court overturned that stay. Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers said in court filings late yesterday.

stories.title: Taxpayer loss after asylum accommodation deals ended
stories.summary: There has been a "substantial loss" to taxpayers, as a result of the termination of agreements with a number of potential asylum seeker accommodation providers. Specific figures in relation to the losses are not contained in today's report from the Comptroller and Auditor General, but there are indications that they could amount to several million euro. The C&AG says financial settlements to three parties form a "material but undisclosed part" of €35 million in accrued expenses by the Department of Justice last year, in respect of accommodation for international protection applicants. A further two prospective providers are taking legal action over the termination of agreements by the State. Chapter 14 of the report examines the cancellation of the pre-contract deals, after the Department decided to curtail the size of the international protection property portfolio and reduce it over time last year. Prior to this happening, agreements had been made with providers in respect of fifteen properties around the country.

stories.title: VFI say morale amongst rural publicans at rock bottom
stories.summary: Morale amongst rural publicans is at rock bottom as pubs continue to close and costs continue to rise, according to the president of the Vintners' Federation of Ireland (VFI). Members of the VFI, a body representing thousands of publicans across Ireland, gathered outside Leinster House this morning in a last-ditch plea to the Government to introduce a new tax credit to support struggling rural pubs in Budget 2027. The VFI's proposed on-trade sustainability scheme is a tax credit of €20 for every 50-litre keg of draught beer or cider sold, capped at €20,000 per pub per year. VFI President Michael O'Donovan said the tax credit would be a lifeline for pubs in rural Ireland. He said: "As we've seen over the last 20 years, pubs in rural Ireland have been disproportionately affected with costs and closures. "So today is a final plea for rural Ireland to save our pubs and to give us a tax break to try and help them survive into the future.

stories.title: Paramount gets court green light on Warner Bros deal
stories.summary: A US judge has entered an order allowing Paramount to ‌close its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros, ending a months-long holdup, as the company named Mattel's Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO to help run the combined business. US District Court Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín approved a September 21 settlement with a California-led group of 12 states that had sued to block one of the largest media mergers in history, saying it would create a media behemoth capable of driving up film and TV prices. Under the settlement, the ⁠combined company must release at least 30 films a year in US cinemas for five years and spend an extra $300m a year on US production. Falling short of the film quota could force it to sell Miramax. It must also negotiate basic cable deals separately for the two companies' channels and create a board of journalists to oversee CBS News and CNN. Groups opposed to the merger objected strongly to the settlement, with some urging the court to reject it. Martínez-Olguín called the deal a "reasonable factual and legal resolution," saying objectors' hopes for the decree "to reach farther - to achieve more - do not rise to the level of legal violations" warranting rejection.

stories.title: Iran says it receives US response to latest proposal
stories.summary: Iran has said it had received a US response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire in the Gulf, days after President Donald ⁠Trump said he had rejected it. Iran's allies were celebrating after Washington withdrew the last of its forces from neighbouring Iraq, where 4,500 US troops died in the biggest US war of the century. More than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed in chaos unleashed after US forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003. Tehran views the pullout as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups, and a step towards its aim of driving US forces out of the region. With the US-Israeli war against Iran now entering its eighth month, Iran put forward a proposal last week under which the United States would lift its blockade of Iranian ports and Iran would reopen the disrupted Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Mr Trump said on Sunday he had rejected the proposal, although Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran had not received a formal rejection.

stories.title: Second row O'Tighearnaigh on juggling medicine and rugby
stories.summary: Conor O'Tighearnaigh could be said to represent something of a throwback. Back in the days when playing rugby was officially a hobby for even those at the highest level, there were plenty of doctors and would-be doctors in the international game. Ireland's greatest player of the pre-professional era, Jack Kyle, worked as a surgeon in Africa for decades. In the professional era, the likes of Felipe Contepomi and Jamie Roberts have combined medical studies with a rugby career. But it's a rare enough combo these days, making Leinster second row O'Tighearnaigh's juggling of the two all the more notable, especially as he attempts to break into the starting team. The 23-year old former St Michael's student, who was part of the Ireland Under-20 Grand Slam winning teams in 2022 and 2023, featured in the pack in Leinster's narrow loss to the Lions in Johannesburg last week. The trip to South Africa has forced a slight pause in his medical training, where he is currently on placement at St Vincent's hospital in Dublin - but he'll catch up soon enough. "I'm now doing it on a stretched-out basis," O'Tighearnaigh said. "I did the first four years full whack. Last year, I took a leave of absence from medicine.

stories.title: Retiring Grugan happy to complete Armagh circle
stories.summary: Rory Grugan's Armagh career started 15 years ago with 70 minutes of McKenna Cup action and his manager Paddy O'Rourke using his post-match media scrum to compare him to Marty Clarke. The Down leftie was one of the hottest names in football at the time, having come so close to dragging the Mourne County to a shock All-Ireland a few months previously. As far as potential player correlations go, it seemed a heavy burden to place on the Ballymacnab youngster. Now as the All-Ireland winner tries to adapt to life without county football - something that's been present in nearly half of his 35 years on this earth - O'Rourke can take solace from being right. Grugan was a linchpin of Armagh's acceleration under Kieran McGeeney, moving from a side that yo-yoed between Division 2 and 3 to being deemed one of the best in the country over the last five years, with Celtic Cross and Ulster medals to show for it. All things come to an end though and with Grugan and fellow 2009 All-Ireland Minor winner James Morgan departing, and more to come in the coming weeks, that 2024 team has lost a lot of names, albeit the Crossmaglen defender left the squad mid-season in '24 before returning last year. After the 2025 campaign, Stefan Campbell, Jemar Hall, Ciaron O'Hanlon (now coached by Clarke at Killeavy), Niall Rowland, Ciaran Higgins and Shane McPartlan all stepped away too.

stories.title: FAI to defend move to play Israel before committee
stories.summary: The FAI is to tell the Oireachtas Sports Committee how the decision to proceed with the controversial fixtures against Israel was made in the best interests of Irish football. The CEO of the FAI David Courell and other senior figures at the Association will answer questions from TDs and Senators this afternoon with Ireland to play Israel again on Sunday in the UEFA Nations League after preparations for last weekend's fixture in Hungary were thrown into chaos at the eleventh hour. Opposition parties have said members of the FAI leadership team should consider their positions over their handling of the games with People Before Profit TD Ruth Coppinger telling the Dáil yesterday how the board and CEO of the FAI should all resign. However, in his opening address to the Oireachtas Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport, Mr Courell is expected to strongly defend the Association's actions. "[The decision] was not an endorsement of Israel's participation or a dismissal of deeply held views across the country. It was a difficult institutional decision made in the interests of Irish football as a whole," Mr Courell will state. "Our responsibility is to protect players, staff and supporters, and the programmes and structures on which football communities depend. We hope the committee understands that fulfilling these fixtures reflects our duty to safeguard the stability and sustainability of Irish football for current and future generations," he will tell TDs and Senators.

stories.title: An unhappy medium: John O'Donnell's new Drama On One play
stories.summary: Fortune-tellers, mediums, psychics: do they really have a connection with the spirit world, or are they charlatans exploiting the vulnerabilities of others? I had been inclined to dismiss them as chancers. However, when I read Hilary Mantel’s Beyond Black, a wickedly funny novel about a troubled psychic, I changed my mind. Maybe it’s not just their customers who feel depressed or unloved; maybe there’s no such thing as a happy medium. I started to explore the insecurities and desires of spiritualists and crystal-gazers. Some were – and are – tatty remnants of the vaudeville age, end-of-the-pier performers at the end of an era. But others do what they do not simply to make money, but to feel needed; to please. Where, I wondered, would a lonely clairvoyant go if she wanted to feel appreciated and loved? A bereavement therapy counselling session seemed the obvious place: and so, we first meet Fidelma, the main character in Horace, among her new 'friends' in the Grief Encounter group.. Horace is the teddy-bear Fidelma brings with her, a theatrical prop designed to endear her to strangers, to win hearts and unsuspecting minds. For a play about hearing voices, radio seems a particularly appropriate format; the perfect medium, you might say. Is Fidelma a misguided nuisance, or irredeemably evil? You’ll have to listen to the play and decide for yourself. But in earlier times a woman like Fidelma might have been condemned as a witch. The cartoon image of pointy hats and cats and spells may have evaporated, but in some places suspicions remain. The last prosecution in Britain under the 1735 Witchcraft Act was only eighty years ago. (Fidelma’s surname, Dunmore, is a nod to ‘The Dunmore Witch’, Alice Kyteler, the first woman charged with witchcraft in Ireland in 1324). Fidelma’s loneliness is at the dark heart of Horace, as is the sometimes desperate need of the bereaved to make contact with a lost loved one; though there are, I hope, moments of black humour also. And for a play about hearing voices, radio seems a particularly appropriate format; the perfect medium, you might say.

stories.title: Lorraine Kelly leads tributes to 'pioneer' Esther Rantzen
stories.summary: Lorraine Kelly and singer Elaine Paige are among the stars paying tribute to "pioneer and force of nature" Esther Rantzen. The broadcaster and campaigner has been remembered following her death aged 86. A statement released by her family remembered her as "the most wonderful mother" and a "cherished grandmother," and her TV work and activism have been remembered by many famous faces and public figures. Rantzen started her career as a broadcaster and became a household name after hosting shows such as That’s Life!, and later established charities to help the young and old. After being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, she also became a prominent voice in the attempt to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales. Paige led the tributes and shared an old photograph of herself smiling alongside Dame Esther to Instagram, writing: "So very sad to hear of the death of Esther Rantzen.

stories.title: Lopez sits front row for Stella McCartney's rain-soaked show
stories.summary: Jennifer Lopez sat front row for Stella McCartney’s rainy spring/summer 2027 show at Paris Fashion Week. It was apt weather for the en plein air show, which had the theme "under the sea". The 57-year-old US singer and actor arrived wearing a faux-fur shawl over the British designer’s layered Sable midi dress and a black veil, sitting with an umbrella front row. After horses trotted alongside models at McCartney’s autumn/winter show earlier this year, the lifelong animal rights campaigner turned her attention from land to sea. The collection explored marine life and the fashion industry’s relationship with animals. Ahead of the show, McCartney shared a film featuring marine biologist and oceanographer Sylvia Earle, who said the collection invited viewers "beneath the blue into a world where humans are not above nature but immersed within the systems".

stories.title: Proposed Drumcree deal 'not acceptable', says DUP MP
stories.summary: A solution to the stand-off over the Orange Order parade at Drumcree hangs in the balance this morning as representatives for Garvaghy Road residents and the Order return to Hillsborough Castle for further talks. Talks with Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant yesterday led to a document which the residents said they could accept, however loyalist sources said they are not acceptable. Mr Bryant has been trying to strike a compromise deal between the two sides of the stand-off. A possible deal emerged out of the blue yesterday, which residents of the Garvaghy Road said they would accept if the Orange Order did. Residents were briefed on the outline at a public meeting last night but details were not released to the media. The proposal seems to have landed better with nationalists than with unionists.

stories.title: €6m Capital Fund announced for arts and culture sector
stories.summary: Details of a new €6 million Arts Capital Investment Fund for the Arts and Culture sector have been announced by Minister for Culture, Patrick O'Donovan. The Minister launched the new pilot capital funding scheme at the Mermaid Arts Centre in Bray, and it was confirmed that it will open for applications tomorrow, 1 October. Speaking at the launch the Minster said that with the fund "we are helping to ensure that arts can play an important part in people's lives, regardless of where you live or your background." This pilot initiative delivers on a Programme for Government commitment to explore a dedicated capital scheme for arts and culture facilities. The €6 million Arts Capital Investment Fund will support arts and culture facilities and organisations throughout the country to purchase equipment and undertake refurbishment works including climate action upgrades, health and safety upgrades and works to provide universal access. This pilot scheme will also support community and voluntary groups with funding for equipment to increase participation in arts and culture.

stories.title: Burnham's big ideas ignite the Labour foot soldiers
stories.summary: He didn't say "let's rejoin the EU". He didn't even say "let's join the single market". But Andy Burnham did tell his first Labour Party Conference as UK Prime Minister that Brexit has not given Britain back control, and has done more harm than good to the UK economy. It was a speech that distilled the essence of Labour - bottled, packaged and marketed for the 21st Century. But Mr Burnham's promises on social care, housing, employment, pensions and utilities all need money. Tax money. That can only come from a growing economy. And one of the engines of growth, as Mr Burnham sees it, is the European Union - still Britain's biggest trade partner and market, but, after Brexit, not delivering what it could for British business. And if it is not delivering for business and employment, it is not delivering the taxes they yield to the government. Hence, the pressing need for a new relationship with the EU. Promising to put an end to a "decade of divisiveness and drift," Mr Burnham said: "We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market". This is what is at stake at the several-times delayed EU-UK summit that both sides say they want to happen before the end of the year. Mr Burnham and Taoiseach Micheál Martin spoke about it at their meeting in Manchester last week. Mr Martin would like it to happen during the Irish Presidency.

stories.title: How historical taxes helped shaped the buildings around us
stories.summary: Analysis: The buildings around us can have been influenced by tax avoidance as generations of property owners adapted their homes in reaction to the system From the size of the bricks used for building to houses squeezed into impossibly narrow plots, architecture has often been shaped by taxation just as much as by creativity and taste. As we approach the next annual budget, let's look back at some historic taxes that have left visible legacies on the architecture we see around us. A window tax was introduced in Ireland in 1799, levied on the number of windows in a dwelling house. It was payable by the occupier of the house and applied to every inhabited dwelling-house in Ireland. All windows in occupied houses were subject to the tax including skylights, staircase lights, garret and passage lights. The legislation provided an exemption for 'any window occupied with or used for a loom which shall be standing at such window, and be really used for weaving’, the wording clearly anticipating attempts to avoid the tax by placing a loom in every window. While the window tax is commonly blamed for the existence of blind windows in Georgian buildings in England, there is little evidence that windows were bricked up to avoid the tax in Ireland. In fact, the tax was levied on windows that existed in the house on 1 January 1799, predating the implementation of the tax and preventing occupiers from avoiding the tax by blocking up the windows after the tax was introduced. It is more likely that the number of windows in houses built after the introduction of the tax were carefully planned to reduce the liability. The window tax was accused of levying ‘a tax upon daylight’ which is said to have resulted in the phrase ‘daylight robbery’, though this is contested. The British brick tax was introduced in 1784 to help pay for the war with colonial America and was extended to Ireland in 1826. It was levied on the number of bricks in a building. The tax resulted in brick manufacturers making larger bricks to reduce the tax burden as the tax was levied on each brick regardless of size. The British government responded by legally limiting the maximum size of a brick. However, houses built in Ireland and Britian in the late 18th and early 19th centuries with larger bricks or with alternative materials like stone masonry are reminders of a tax that has been long repealed. Indeed, brick size is still used as an effective archaeological dating tool.

stories.title: Passengers describe 'rollercoaster' flydubai flight
stories.summary: A passenger who was on board a plane that was diverted after a co-pilot reportedly attacked the pilot and tried to crash the plane has said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon, who was on the flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, said the co-pilot "tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane". It was like "we were having very big turbulence, but there was no turbulence", passenger Almog Italie told AFP, describing the sensation of losing thousands of feet of altitude in seconds as similar to riding a "rollercoaster". She spoke to reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him," she said. "There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do."

stories.title: Klopp reluctant to weigh in on City fallout
stories.summary: Former Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp said his respect for Pep Guardiola and the Manchester City sides that battled Liverpool in some of the Premier League's closest title races has left him reluctant to comment on the fallout from City's financial rules case. City were found guilty of serious financial breaches by an independent commission on Tuesday, though the club have denied wrongdoing and are expected to appeal, with sanctions yet to be determined. The 59-year-old, whose Liverpool side twice finished a point behind City, had previously joked that he would attend a parade if Liverpool were retrospectively awarded titles but said he no longer felt that way. "I haven't given it much thought, even though I've seen it of course," Klopp told reporters on Wednesday. "I also know what I said about it in the past and how if there's ever a parade I'll be there, but it doesn't feel like that anymore. "My respect for Pep Guardiola and the football played at City during the time we played against each other... plus what an opponent they proved to be for us at the very highest level is far too great for me to be able to say anything now."
